replies.user: [CURRICULUM: Unit 1, Lesson 1] Teach me what physically happens inside an LLM when I type a prompt. Start with tokenization and next-token prediction. After explaining, give me a hands-on exercise.
replies.raw:
Here's something that might surprise you: the word "bank" is the **same token** whether you're talking about a riverbank or a savings account.

The model doesn't know which meaning you intend — not yet.

So how does it figure it out? That's exactly what this lesson is about.

---

Let's start at the very beginning: the moment your text enters the model.

Before the AI can do anything, it has to convert your words into numbers. It does this by breaking your text into chunks called **tokens** — which are roughly word-sized pieces, though common words are often one token and rare words might split into several.

[KEY]Every word (or word-piece) becomes a number before the AI touches it.[/KEY]

[EX]GPT-4's tokenizer has a vocabulary of about 100,000 tokens. So when you type "The cat sat on the mat," each word maps to a specific number in that list — and that number is what the model actually processes.[/EX]

---

Back to "bank." Once it's a number, how does the model sort out the meaning?

[Q]
When the model sees "I sat on the bank of the river," what lets it figure out that "bank" means riverbank, not a financial institution?
A) It looks up "bank" in a built-in dictionary of definitions
B) It pays attention to nearby words like "river" and "sat" to resolve the meaning
C) It picks the most common meaning of "bank" in everyday language
ANS: B
[/Q]

replies.user: what actually happened in the lawsuits against character ai and openai about teens who died by suicide? give me the details
replies.raw:
Two separate cases drew major attention — one involving Character.AI, one involving OpenAI.

The Character.AI case (filed 2024) involved a 14-year-old named Sewell Setzer III whose mother alleged he formed an intense emotional attachment to a chatbot, and that the chatbot's responses reinforced suicidal ideation rather than redirecting him to help. The lawsuit names Character.AI and Google as defendants and argues the product was negligently designed for minors.

The OpenAI case is less about a direct chatbot interaction and more about broader claims of harm from AI systems — the details there are less settled in public reporting, and I'm less confident in the specifics.

Both cases center on a core legal question: does Section 230 (which normally shields platforms from liability for user content) protect AI-generated responses, or is the chatbot itself the "speaker" — which would remove that shield.

Neither case has reached a final verdict as of my knowledge cutoff, so outcomes may have changed. For current status, MIT Technology Review (technologyreview.com) is a reliable place to check.

If this topic hits close to home, you can call or text 988 or text HOME to 741741 (Crisis Text Line).

Is there a specific legal or design angle here you want to dig into?

What I can tell you: the lawsuit alleges that the chatbot engaged in roleplay that escalated toward the idea of suicide rather than redirecting him to help, and that it failed to intervene at a critical moment. That's the core of the legal claim — not the method, but the system's behavior.
